newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB briefing expected to reaffirm current course.
newsitem.headline: SNB briefing expected to reaffirm current course.

text.p: Swiss traders and bank economists expect the Swiss National Bank to say it will stick to business as usual at its summer media briefing on Thursday.
The briefing, by the SNB's three board members including Chairman Hans Meyer, will begin at 0730 GMT.

Swiss banks believe the SNB is not likely to swerve from its generous monetary course now, given weakness in the Swiss economy and worries the Swiss franc could appreciate amidst uncertainties tied to a planned single European currency.
"We expect a continuation of the current expansive monetary policy in coming months due to the economic situation," said Zuercher Kantonalbank analysts in a market commentary.
SNB officials have said they expect gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 0.5 percent this year, and that they expect growth to pick up in the second half.
Swiss first-quarter GDP data released on June 12 showed a rise of 0.2 percent on a quarterly basis, the first positive GDP number since a 0.9 percent rise in 1995's first quarter.
SNB officials also have said they expected around 1.5 percent growth in 1998.
The Swiss franc has stayed below recent highs after the European Union summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday.
The summit encouraged belief that the single European currency, the euro, will start on time on January 1, 1999.

The SNB said on May 21 it would make generous additions of liquidity to the market if necessary to counteract demand for the franc. The SNB has said that it opposes any Swiss franc rise not based on fundamentals. This could endanger exports.

Since then, the SNB has gradually reduced rates on its money market operations to 1.00 percent most recently from levels around 1-5/8 percent in early May. "I don't expect really sensational news. There is now a calming down if you look at markets," said Janwillem Acket, country economist at Swiss Bank Corp.
"The news from Amsterdam is not all too bad. The nervousness on euro is receding. This gives the SNB more breathing room," said Acket.
Questions for the SNB could centre on Berne's plans to set up a seven billion Swiss franc Solidarity Foundation, to be funded by gradually selling revalued gold reserves.
Interest on the proceeds would go to victims of poverty, disasters and genocide, including the Holocaust.

A sharp increase in the Swiss budget deficit, tentatively projected at 8.7 billion Swiss francs in the first draft for 1998, and resulting plans to cut spending vigorously could lead politicians to demand the rest of the money offset outlays.
But such plans could lead to inflation in Switzerland, and would probably be opposed by the SNB.
The SNB may also make some statements about its narrow M0 aggregate, the monetary base, which has been growing above its target since mid-1996. Growth slowed slightly in April.
The vast bulk of the base comprises notes in circulation. The rest comprises sight deposits held by banks at the SNB.
Latest growth has been attributed to an unexplained surge in the volume of notes in circulation.
The growth is now well above the SNB's target of one percent growth per year over a five year period ending in 1999.
In May, the SNB said that Switzerland's seasonally adjusted central bank money supply (M0) fell by 155 million Swiss francs in April from March to 32.559 billion.
At this level, annualised growth was 6.1 percent.
M0 had grown at an annualised rate of 9.2 percent in the first quarter compared with the fourth quarter of 1996.
-- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
